JPG, PNG or WebP: Which Image Format Should You Use for Online Forms?

By Kamlesh Mohabe, Software Engineer · Published 2026-10-04

Which format to choose for forms and uploads, how each handles small file sizes and transparency, and why JPEG is usually the safe option.

Question: What is the difference between the formats?

JPEG and WebP are lossy formats. They reduce file size by discarding detail that is hard to see. PNG is lossless. It stores every pixel exactly, which gives sharp edges but larger files for photos. WebP can be lossy or lossless and supports transparency.

Question: Which should I use for a passport-style photo?

JPEG. It is accepted almost everywhere, it handles photographs efficiently, and it can reach small targets such as 20 or 50 KB when you also reduce dimensions sensibly.

Question: Which for a signature?

Forms usually ask for JPEG here as well. A signature is simple, so it compresses very well. If the form accepts PNG, it will keep the lines crisp, but at the cost of a bigger file.

Question: When is PNG better?

For logos, charts, screenshots of text and images with transparency. If the form allows PNG and the limit is generous, PNG avoids compression artefacts. For a tiny limit like 20 KB, a photo as PNG will almost never fit.

Question: Is WebP a good idea?

WebP often gives a smaller file than JPEG at similar quality, which helps with strict limits. But many older systems and some government portals only accept JPG or PNG. If the form does not list WebP, do not use it.

Question: Does converting change quality?

Converting a photo to JPEG or WebP is lossy, so keep the original. Converting JPEG to PNG does not restore lost detail. It only makes the file larger. Compress once, from the best source you have.

Question: What happens to transparency?

JPEG has no transparency. When you convert a transparent PNG to JPEG, transparent areas become white in this tool. If the picture will be placed on a coloured background, use PNG or WebP when the form allows it.

A simple rule

If the form says JPG or JPEG, use JPEG. If it does not say, use JPEG for photos and PNG for graphics. Check the downloaded file extension matches the real format. ImageTo20KB only names a file .jpg when it is genuinely a JPEG.

Examples from everyday uploads

A passport-style photo of a face usually fits a 20–50 KB range as a JPEG once cropped and resized, while the same photo as PNG would be many times larger. A scanned signature may be only a few KB as JPEG and might even be fine as PNG if the limit allows. A screenshot of a bank statement with small text is better kept as PNG at a larger size, or as a high-quality WebP if the portal accepts it. A company logo with a transparent background should stay PNG. When two formats are allowed, compare the sizes in the result card and choose the one that is both small and sharp.

If your device saves photos in a format your form does not accept, such as HEIC, export or convert to JPG on the device first, since this tool does not read HEIC files.
